items.text: Grief and relief after a late diagnosis don't take turns. They arrive together. Feeling devastated about lost years and grateful for answers — sometimes in the same hour — isn't regression. That's exactly what the research shows.
items.rationale: Names the core finding of the Mair et al. 2026 'grief, relief, and belief' study in plain language; validates an experience many late-diagnosed adults describe but rarely see named anywhere.

items.text: There's pressure to skip straight to gratitude after a late diagnosis. But grief for your younger self isn't going backward. It's the processing. It's what actually moves you forward.
items.rationale: Distinct companion to the validation post — reframes grief as a necessary phase rather than a problem to overcome; works as an evergreen reframe without repeating the study statistic.

items.text: For many autistic and ADHD workers, remote work wasn't a perk. It was the accommodation. RTO mandates withdrew it without process, without conversation, without even using the word 'accommodation.'
items.rationale: Reframes a structural policy story as a personal one using the Fortune May 2026 reporting; gives neurodivergent workers precise language for what happened to them.

items.text: If your company is calling people back in and you're neurodivergent: remote work can be a formal accommodation, not just a preference. HR may not mention that unprompted. You're allowed to ask.
items.rationale: Translates the RTO-as-accommodation-withdrawal reframe into a concrete step workers may not know is available to them; actionable rather than just validating.
items.sensitivity_flag: Accommodation rights vary by jurisdiction and employer size — broadly accurate under US ADA and UK Equality Act 2010 but not universal. Readers should verify locally.

items.text: Demand avoidance in PDA isn't defiance. A 2026 study found it tracks anxiety directly — the harder demands push, the worse the nervous system loop gets. That's not a willpower failure. It's a threat response.
items.rationale: Addresses the most common and damaging misread of PDA using 2026 Rai et al. findings; speaks to parents, educators, and PDA adults who were punished for what was a nervous system response.

items.text: 72% of neurodivergent workers mask at work. That's a second job — invisible, uncompensated, exhausting — running parallel to the actual job. Nobody clocks out of it at 5pm.
items.rationale: The 'second job' framing converts a private exhaustion into a structural injustice; the Understood 2026 survey statistic grounds the claim precisely without overstating it.

items.text: What would it feel like to actually clock out of masking — not someday, not in some ideal job, but just once this week, in one conversation, with someone safe enough?
items.rationale: Follows the masking micro-insight with an inviting, low-stakes question rather than leaving it as pure critique; specificity ('this week', 'one conversation') makes it genuinely answerable.

items.text: Regulation starts with recognition. If someone can't accurately sense their own internal state, 'just calm down' isn't bad advice — it's the wrong tool entirely. You can't regulate what you can't feel.
items.rationale: Translates the interoception concept into a punchy, non-clinical insight; moves regulation conversations from behaviour management to body literacy in two sentences.

items.text: AuDHD burnout often doesn't look like collapse. It looks like fine. A slow narrowing — less capacity, less tolerance, less joy — months before anything appears wrong from the outside.
items.rationale: Validates the quiet-erosion pattern that gets dismissed precisely because it looks okay externally; 'it looks like fine' is the recognition many AuDHD adults have been waiting to see named.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't 'no rules.' It's removing threat from structure. Safety isn't indulgence — it's the prerequisite for everything else.
items.rationale: Condenses the live PDA parenting debate into a single distinction that separates 'removing threat' from 'removing all structure'; directly addresses the 'permissiveness' criticism without being defensive.

items.text: What's one demand you could offer as a choice this week instead? Not a trick, not a reward chart. Just: here are two ways this could happen — which works for you?
items.rationale: Bridges the low-demand reframe into a practical, genuinely accessible invitation for parents and adults alike; the concreteness lowers the barrier to actually trying it.

items.text: Accommodation requests jumped from 24% to 33% in two years. And 60% of neurodivergent employees still don't know who to ask — up from 49% last year. The need is growing faster than the path.
items.rationale: Two numbers moving in opposite directions surface a structural irony that invites both personal stories and systemic commentary; the closing line names the tension without editorializing.
